title: About pacemaker implantation | NHS inform
text:
About pacemaker implantation
Pacemaker implantation is a procedure to put a small electrical device called a pacemaker into your chest. The pacemaker sends regular electrical impulses, which help keep your heart beating regularly.
Fitting a pacemaker is one of the most common heart procedures.
How does a pacemaker work?
A pacemaker is a small metal box that weighs 20 to 50g. It’s attached to one or more wires, known as pacing leads, that run to your heart.
A pacemaker contains:
a battery which usually lasts from 8 to 10 years
an impulse generator
a tiny computer circuit
The tiny computer circuit turns energy from the battery into electrical impulses. These flow down the wires and stimulate your heart to contract. The rate at which these electrical pulses are sent is called the discharge rate.
Almost all modern pacemakers work on demand. This means that they can be programmed to adjust the discharge rate in response to your body’s needs. If the pacemaker senses that your heart has missed a beat or is beating too slowly, it sends signals at a steady rate. If it senses that your heart is beating normally by itself, it doesn’t send out any signals.
Most pacemakers have a special sensor that recognises body movement or breathing rate. This allows them to speed up the discharge rate when you’re active. This is described as rate-responsive.
Why do I need a pacemaker?
The heart is essentially a pump, made of muscle, which is controlled by electrical signals. These signals can get interrupted by various things. This can lead to several dangerous heart conditions like a:
slow heart beat (bradycardia), an abnormally fast heartbeat (
supraventricular tachycardia
), or sometimes both
heart block
– when the electrical impulses that control the beating of the heart muscle are disrupted
cardiac arrest –when the heart stops pumping blood around your body
Implantable Cardioverter Defibrillator (ICD)
An implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) is a device similar to a pacemaker.
It sends a larger electrical shock to the heart that “reboots” it to get it pumping again. Some modern devices contain both a pacemaker and an ICD.
ICDs are often used as a preventative treatment for people who are thought to be at risk of cardiac arrest. If the ICD senses that the heart is beating at a potentially dangerous abnormal rate, it will deliver an electrical shock to the heart. This can often help return the heart to a normal rhythm.
Find out more about ICDs
Complications of pacemaker implantation
As with any medical or surgical procedure, pacemaker implantation has risks as well as benefits. The complications of pacemaker implantation can include:
pacemaker infection – there’s a small risk that the site of the pacemaker, ICD, or their leads can become infected
pacemaker malfunction – there is a small chance that your pacemaker could stop working properly
twiddler’s syndrome – when the pacemaker generator is pulled out of its normal position
